description: Gold 20 completion reviews for bounded work and learning protocols. These source reviews preserve practical evidence boundaries and reference existing passing structured retrieval cases.

30-minute-deadline-sprints.user_problem: A low-risk task keeps expanding through polishing or delay, and I need a bounded rough first pass without pretending speed can replace essential quality checks.
eligibility: The task is low-risk and reversible enough that an imperfect first pass has real value.
The user can define a minimum useful output and separate required content from optional polish.
Any factual, safety, legal, financial, medical, security, or other essential verification can still happen before the work is shared or acted on.
when_not_to_use: Do not manufacture time pressure for safety-critical, legal, medical, financial, security, compliance, or other work where rushing can create material harm.
Do not use the timebox to hide required checks, approvals, dependencies, or context that must be present before the output is usable.
Do not treat thirty minutes or any other exact duration as a scientifically established productivity optimum.
30-minute-deadline-sprints.first_action: Define the minimum useful first-pass output, write down what can wait until revision, and choose a shorter-than-usual work boundary that still leaves essential checks intact.
steps: Choose a low-risk task where a rough first pass is genuinely useful, such as an outline, draft, sketch, brief, or early analysis.
Write the minimum useful output before starting so the timebox protects a concrete artifact rather than vague activity.
Remove optional formatting, extra examples, polish, or secondary sections while preserving anything needed for accuracy, safety, or understanding.
Work until the chosen boundary, simplifying scope rather than silently lowering essential standards when time is short.
At the boundary, record what remains and stop or deliberately choose a revision pass instead of calling the draft finished by default.
Before sharing or acting on the result, complete the factual, contextual, tone, approval, and other quality checks the task actually requires.

review_horizon.value: At the end of the first-pass boundary and again before the work is shared or acted on
review_horizon.rationale: The first review tests whether the constraint created a useful artifact and clearer scope decisions; the second prevents a draft boundary from being confused with final quality.

30-minute-deadline-sprints.observable_signal: Whether a concrete first-pass artifact exists, optional scope was explicitly deferred, essential checks remained visible, and the user can state what still needs revision before use.
30-minute-deadline-sprints.stop_or_change_rule: Lengthen or abandon the timebox when it repeatedly creates stress without useful scope decisions, hides required work, or pressures the user to skip essential verification. Reduce scope rather than reduce safety or correctness.
30-minute-deadline-sprints.fallback: If a timer adds pressure without helping, define a minimum useful untimed draft or choose the smallest concrete next section, produce that, and review what remains.

evidence_boundary.statement: This is a low-risk editorial timeboxing template. Brali does not attach reviewed evidence establishing thirty minutes, a shorter deadline, or this exact sequence as an optimal productivity or creativity intervention.

limitations: The exact duration is an organizational convenience rather than an evidence-backed dose.
Finishing a first pass does not establish that the work is accurate, complete, useful, or ready to share.
Time pressure can degrade quality or judgment when a task is complex, consequential, or poorly scoped.
A personally useful timebox does not demonstrate a general productivity effect.
30-minute-deadline-sprints.agent_summary: Use this for a reversible first pass: define the minimum useful artifact, defer optional polish, work to a short boundary, then review before sharing. Treat the duration as adjustable and never trade essential accuracy or safety checks for speed.

2-minute-desk-tidy-timer.user_problem: My immediate workspace is creating small physical friction before the next task, and I want a tiny reset that does not turn cleaning into another form of procrastination.
eligibility: A small part of the workspace is physically cluttered or inconvenient for the next ordinary low-risk task.
The user can make a few obvious moves without starting a larger organizing or disposal decision.
The user is willing to stop once the next task is easier to begin rather than pursuing a perfectly tidy environment.
when_not_to_use: Do not use a desk-reset ritual to avoid the actual task when the workspace is already usable.
Do not rush the handling of hazardous materials, confidential papers, valuable equipment, medication, or anything else that requires deliberate storage or disposal.
Do not treat two minutes or a tidy desk as an evidence-backed productivity requirement.
2-minute-desk-tidy-timer.first_action: Choose the smallest workspace area needed for the next task, set a short stopping boundary if useful, and make only obvious moves that clear immediate physical friction.
steps: Pick one small area such as the keyboard space, one corner of the desk, or the area around the material needed next.
Use a short boundary only to keep the reset small; two minutes is a convenient default rather than a required duration.
Make obvious moves such as removing trash, moving a cup, returning an item with a clear home, or stacking papers that block the surface.
Avoid opening new drawers, redesigning storage, or starting decisions that turn the reset into a larger organizing project.
Stop once the area is usable enough and immediately begin the real task the reset was meant to support.
After several uses, keep the ritual only if it reduces friction more often than it becomes avoidance.

review_horizon.value: Immediately after the reset, with a broader check after several uses
review_horizon.rationale: The immediate signal is whether the next task became easier to start; repeated use reveals whether the reset is useful or merely another ritual.

2-minute-desk-tidy-timer.observable_signal: Whether the intended work area became usable, the reset stayed small, and the user moved into the real task rather than extending the cleanup.
2-minute-desk-tidy-timer.stop_or_change_rule: Stop or shorten the reset when the workspace is already usable, the ritual repeatedly delays work, or the items require deliberate decisions rather than obvious moves. Schedule deeper cleaning separately when it is genuinely needed.
2-minute-desk-tidy-timer.fallback: Skip the timer and make one obvious move that removes the main obstruction, or start the task as-is when tidying would add more friction than it removes.

evidence_boundary.statement: This is a low-risk environmental reset template. Brali does not claim that two minutes, tidiness, or this exact sequence produces a reliable improvement in productivity, focus, or wellbeing.

limitations: Two minutes is not an evidence-backed optimum.
A cleaner workspace can still leave the real blocker, task ambiguity, or dependency unchanged.
The ritual can become procrastination if it expands beyond the immediate area or is repeated unnecessarily.
A user's subjective sense of reduced friction does not establish a causal productivity effect.
2-minute-desk-tidy-timer.agent_summary: Use this only as a tiny workspace reset: clear one small area with obvious moves, stop before organizing expands, and begin the real task. Two minutes is optional, and the method is useful only if it reduces rather than adds friction.

weekly-theme-learning-sprints.user_problem: My learning is scattered across too many topics and resources, and I need one narrow weekly practice target with a visible result and a simple way to learn from friction.
eligibility: The learner can choose one narrow low-risk skill or topic that can be practiced through small attempts during the week.
A visible end-of-week artifact or demonstration can represent progress without pretending to measure mastery.
The learner can reduce scope when the week gets crowded and can inspect errors, friction, or unanswered questions after practice.
when_not_to_use: Do not treat one week, a daily streak, or a fixed number of practice sessions as a scientifically optimal learning schedule.
Do not use a narrow weekly theme as a substitute for qualified supervision, feedback, or assessment where errors are high stakes.
Do not spend the week collecting resources when the target requires actual recall, production, problem solving, or performance practice.
weekly-theme-learning-sprints.first_action: Choose one narrow learning theme and one visible end-of-week artifact, then make the first small practice attempt before collecting more resources.
steps: Name a skill narrow enough that one visible end-of-week result is realistic.
Choose the end-of-week artifact or demonstration that will make the practice outcome inspectable.
Start each working session with a small attempt and write one sentence about the main friction, error, or uncertainty it exposed.
Use only the resource or feedback needed for that friction, then try another practice rep when useful.
When the week becomes crowded, shrink the artifact or practice scope instead of compensating with an oversized catch-up session.
At the end of the week, review what became easier, what friction repeated, and whether the next theme should continue, narrow, or change.

review_horizon.value: At the end of each practice attempt, with a deliberate review at the end of the week
review_horizon.rationale: Short reviews keep input tied to observed friction; the end-of-week review tests whether the chosen scope produced a useful artifact and a clearer next learning decision.

weekly-theme-learning-sprints.observable_signal: Whether real practice attempts occurred, a visible artifact or demonstration exists, recurring friction is identifiable, and the learner can name a useful next practice decision.
weekly-theme-learning-sprints.stop_or_change_rule: Narrow or replace the theme when the artifact is repeatedly unreachable, practice turns mostly into passive consumption, the material is far too easy or too hard, or feedback needs exceed what self-study can provide.
weekly-theme-learning-sprints.fallback: If a weekly frame adds overhead, choose one small skill and one next practice rep without a weekly commitment, then review that attempt before choosing the next.

evidence_boundary.statement: This is a practical learning-organization template. Brali does not claim that a one-week theme, daily reps, three resources, or this exact loop is an evidence-backed optimal schedule for learning or retention.

limitations: A visible weekly artifact is a planning device, not proof of mastery or durable retention.
The value of the format depends on the quality of practice and feedback, not merely on staying with one theme.
Some skills require longer projects, expert supervision, or richer interaction than a weekly sprint can provide.
The protocol specifies no evidence-backed session duration, repetition count, streak target, or resource limit.
weekly-theme-learning-sprints.agent_summary: Use one narrow weekly theme to reduce scattering: define a visible result, practise before consuming more resources, note friction, and review the week. Shrink scope when needed and treat the weekly frame as a convenience, not a learning dose.
